strengths: The paper studies a well-motivated theoretical problem: online fair division of indivisible goods under different levels of future information. The organization around no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations is coherent and useful.

Several results appear meaningful if correct, especially the normalized-valuations algorithm giving EF1 for two agents and PROP1 for any number of agents, and the general frequency-prediction meta-result for feasible share-based notions. These results connect online fair division to online algorithms with advice/predictions in a natural way.
The paper provides complementary impossibility results in most regimes, which helps clarify the value and limits of each information model rather than only giving positive algorithms.
The manuscript has a broad and mostly relevant related-work discussion, and it explicitly identifies open problems such as EF1 with frequency predictions for three or more agents.
weaknesses: There is at least one serious soundness issue in the proof of Theorem 5.5, the claimed EFX guarantee for two agents with frequency predictions. In the proof, the constructed allocation B appears to have a type/notation error when removing f(g*) from A2, and the subsequent inequality chain contradicts the earlier assumption v_1^{IDO}(A'_1) < v_1^{IDO}(A'_2). This makes a central positive result unsupported as written.

Algorithm 1 is underspecified/incorrect as pseudocode: when N' becomes empty, Line 4 says to allocate all remaining goods to agent 1, but the algorithm then continues to Line 12, which takes an argmax over the empty active set. This may be easy to repair with a break/continue, but as written it affects the formal algorithm used in Theorems 4.1 and 4.2.

Some proofs contain apparent algebraic or logical slips and typos that make verification difficult. For example, in Theorem 4.1 the inequality for goods in A2 is written as v2(g') >= v2(g'), and in Theorem 4.4 the final limit says delta -> 0 where the argument requires delta -> infinity. These may be typographical, but there are enough such issues to reduce confidence.

The frequency-prediction model is very strong: it gives each agent's full multiset of future values and the exact number of future goods. The paper motivates this by analogy to predictions, but it does not discuss robustness to prediction error except as future work, limiting practical significance of the strongest positive results.

Reproducibility is acceptable for a theory paper in the sense that algorithms and proofs are mostly stated, but several algorithms rely on offline existence/computation of allocations or picking sequences without a clear complexity discussion. This is especially relevant for the meta-algorithm over arbitrary feasible shares.

The limitations discussion is brief. The paper notes open questions and noisy predictions as future work, but it does not clearly separate assumptions, computational tractability, and prediction realism as limitations. There are no obvious ethical concerns beyond standard allocation-fairness caveats.

strengths: The paper addresses a natural and timely question in online fair division: how different levels of future information affect guarantees for EF1/EFX/PROP1/MMS. The taxonomy of no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations is useful.

Several negative results are conceptually simple and informative, especially the impossibility statements for approximate EF1/EFX in adversarial online settings. These help clarify how far standard offline fairness notions can be pushed online.

The frequency-prediction section contains an interesting high-level idea: reduce certain online guarantees to offline share-based guarantees via a picking-sequence simulation. If made fully rigorous, this could be a useful conceptual contribution.
The paper is mostly readable and situates itself reasonably well relative to online fair division, semi-online scheduling, and learning-augmented algorithms.
weaknesses: A central positive result appears technically unsound as written. Algorithm 1 can make all agents inactive before Line 12, leaving arg max over an empty active set. A trivial normalized instance with two agents and one good of value 1 for both agents triggers this: both agents satisfy the inactivity condition before the good is allocated. This makes Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 unsupported in their current form.

The proof logic for Algorithm 1 also relies on the good that caused an agent to become inactive being available as an outside witness good. If the current good is later allocated to that same agent, the PROP1/EF1 witness argument need not apply as stated. This is not just a presentation issue; it affects the invariant behind the algorithm.

The frequency-prediction results, especially Theorem 5.5, contain substantial rigor and notation problems. The mapping f between actual goods and IDO goods is ill-defined, the set expression A2 \ {f(g*)} is type-inconsistent, and the argument that the constructed allocation contradicts leximin++ is not convincingly established. Since EFX with frequency predictions is one of the paper's headline claims, this is a serious weakness.

Several proofs contain apparent typos or algebraic/logical slips that make verification difficult, e.g. in Theorem 4.1 the text states v2(g') >= v2(g') where a cross-agent comparison is needed, and in Theorem 4.4 one case concludes with 'as delta -> 0' despite requiring delta -> infinity. These may be fixable, but their frequency reduces confidence in the manuscript's technical reliability.

The paper does not provide enough discussion of computational aspects. Some results are existential via offline feasible shares or picking sequences, but it is unclear when the proposed online algorithms are efficient, especially for broad share-based notions and the frequency-prediction meta-algorithm.

The significance is limited by the strength and realism of the information models. Frequency predictions are assumed perfect and quite rich, while robustness to noisy or erroneous predictions is deferred entirely to future work. This weakens the practical relevance of the strongest positive guarantees.

The limitations discussion is brief and mostly appears in the conclusion. The paper acknowledges noisy predictions and unresolved EF1 under frequency predictions, but does not clearly separate proven guarantees, conjectures, computational feasibility, and model realism. Ethical concerns are minimal for this theoretical topic, but reproducibility is mainly proof-based and currently hampered by the proof gaps above.

strengths: The paper studies a clean and important question: how different kinds of future information affect achievable fairness guarantees in online indivisible-goods allocation. The framing across no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations is coherent and gives a useful map of the landscape.

The main positive results are meaningful. Algorithm 1 gives PROP1 for any number of agents under normalization information and EF1/0.5-MMS for two agents, improving the scope of prior semi-online MMS work. The frequency-prediction meta-algorithm is especially elegant: reducing online guarantees to offline feasible share guarantees is a broad and reusable insight.

The paper provides complementary impossibility results for EF1/EFX/MMS-style guarantees under weaker information assumptions. These lower bounds substantially strengthen the contribution because they clarify which additional information is actually useful and where even strong predictions do not close the online/offline gap.

The work is well situated in fair division, online algorithms with advice/predictions, and semi-online scheduling. The authors also identify and correct a claimed PROP1 impossibility argument from prior work, which is a valuable scholarly contribution.
Reproducibility is adequate for a theory paper: the model, assumptions, algorithms, and adversarial constructions are mostly explicit, and no empirical artifact is needed to reproduce the claims.
weaknesses: The presentation of several proofs and algorithms needs polishing before the paper is fully reliable to build on. Algorithm 1 appears to allocate all remaining goods to agent 1 when the active set is empty but then continues to Line 12, where argmax over an empty active set is undefined. This is likely an easy pseudocode fix, but it is in a central algorithm.

There are multiple notation and proof typos in important sections. For example, Theorem 4.1 has an apparent typo v2(g') >= v2(g') where v1(g') is intended; Theorem 4.4 ends one contradiction with delta -> 0 despite earlier requiring large delta; Algorithm 2 line 5 uses vt+1,IDO_i without clearly applying it to gj; and the proof of Theorem 5.5 contains set notation inconsistencies around f(g*) and some garbled inequality text. These do not obviously invalidate the results, but they create avoidable verification friction.

The frequency-prediction model assumes exact per-agent value multisets and exact item count. This is a strong information model, and the paper could more explicitly discuss its practical plausibility and how sensitive the guarantees are to noisy or misspecified predictions. The conclusion mentions robustness as future work, but the limitation deserves clearer treatment earlier.

The central share-based result is attractive, but the computational aspects are somewhat implicit: the meta-algorithm relies on finding an offline feasible-share allocation/picking sequence, and the paper should state whether the resulting online algorithms are polynomial-time whenever the corresponding offline procedure is polynomial-time, and what happens for shares whose feasibility is existential.

The paper has no explicit research ethics or broader impacts discussion. For this mostly theoretical fair-division work the ethical risks are limited, but allocation algorithms can affect real resource distribution, and the assumptions behind fairness guarantees should be communicated carefully in deployment contexts.

strengths: The paper studies a clean and well-motivated theoretical question: what future information is sufficient for online fair division of indivisible goods. The comparison across no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations gives a coherent map of achievable and impossible guarantees.

The technical contribution is substantial within online fair division. The normalization-information algorithm gives PROP1 for all n and EF1 for n=2, with matching impossibility results for stronger notions. The frequency-prediction meta-algorithm is elegant: it lifts offline share-based guarantees to the online setting and recovers the best known MMS approximation under this richer advice model.

The manuscript is generally well written and self-contained. Definitions are clear, theorem statements are explicit, and the summary table helps readers understand the many regimes and fairness notions. The authors also clarify a flaw in prior PROP1 reasoning and situate the work carefully relative to Zhou et al. and related online fair-division literature.

Reproducibility is adequate for a theory paper: algorithms are given in pseudocode, assumptions are stated, and the proofs appear mostly complete. The paper also discusses randomized algorithms under adaptive adversaries and includes learning-augmented variants for noisy advice.
weaknesses: The ICML relevance is somewhat indirect. The paper is primarily an algorithmic game theory/fair division theory paper, with only light connection to ML systems and learning-augmented algorithms. There is no empirical component or concrete predictive pipeline, and the applications to ML-driven allocation remain motivational rather than technically integrated.

The frequency-prediction model is very strong and may limit practical significance. Knowing each agent's entire multiset of future values, even without order, is close to substantial future information; moreover, the model abstracts away correlations between agents' values on the same item until arrival. This makes the strongest positive results less compelling as realistic online guarantees.

The noisy frequency-prediction result is comparatively weak: the guarantee is parameterized by the realized online instantiation error induced by the algorithm, but the paper does not provide a substantive bound for the suggested nearest-neighbor instantiation rule in terms of a natural prediction distance. As a result, the learning-augmented claim is more of a stability observation than a full prediction-robust algorithmic result.

The scope is broad, but some parts feel less fully resolved. For example, EF1 with frequency predictions for n>=3 is left open, and the identical-valuations section, while interesting, reads more like an additional appendix-style exploration than a central contribution to the main narrative.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. There are no obvious material ethical concerns, but for a paper motivated by allocation in ML systems, it would be useful to discuss how worst-case ex post fairness guarantees interact with strategic behavior, biased forecasts, deployment constraints, or harms from inaccurate predictions.

strengths: The paper studies a well-defined and important theoretical question: what future information is needed to obtain fairness guarantees in online allocation of indivisible goods. The comparison among no information, normalization information, and frequency predictions gives the work a coherent structure.

The manuscript contains several nontrivial positive and negative results, including an EF1/PROP1 algorithm under normalization information, strong impossibility results for EF1/EFX, a general reduction from offline share-based guarantees to online guarantees with frequency predictions, and noisy-advice variants.

The theory is mostly presented constructively: the algorithms are explicit, the assumptions are stated, and the proofs generally proceed with clear invariants or adversarial constructions rather than relying on opaque arguments.
The paper situates itself in a relevant fair-division and online-algorithms literature, including prior work on online fair division, MMS, semi-online scheduling, and learning-augmented algorithms.
weaknesses: The contribution feels more appropriate for algorithmic game theory than for the ICML main track. The ML connection is largely motivational: predictions are assumed as advice, but there is no learning model, no statistical analysis, no empirical validation, and no treatment of how such predictions would be obtained or calibrated in realistic ML systems.

The central novelty is uneven. Some results are useful, but several are extensions, combinations, or refinements of known online fair-division and semi-online scheduling ideas. The frequency-prediction result is elegant, but it relies on a very strong information model that nearly reconstructs the offline value multisets, limiting the conceptual surprise and practical relevance.

The paper overclaims practical motivation relative to what is proven. Applications such as recommendation exposure, compute allocation, and content moderation are invoked, but the model assumes additive utilities, complete immediate valuation observation for each arriving good, and strong future information. The gap between these assumptions and the motivating ML systems is not seriously addressed.

The learning-augmented sections are relatively shallow. The noisy-normalization result mainly rescales existing guarantees, and the noisy-frequency result is parameterized by an instantiation error that the paper does not substantially bound except via a simple closest-match heuristic. Thus the robustness claims are formal but not very informative without additional assumptions.

Soundness appears plausible at a high level, but the manuscript is long and proof-heavy, and some arguments depend on delicate adversarial constructions, tie-breaking, and online instantiation details. The paper would benefit from more explicit discussion of model subtleties such as whether the stream length is known, how early-stopping rules are implemented online, and how frequency predictions encode only marginal value multisets rather than joint item types.

Presentation is dense and sometimes repetitive. The introduction and table are helpful, but the main text spends many pages on proof details while leaving the broader significance, model interpretation, and limitations underdeveloped. Important caveats are scattered rather than synthesized clearly.

Reproducibility is only partial. For a theory paper, the main objects are mostly specified, but there is no artifact, no worked examples beyond lower-bound constructions, and no clear guide for reproducing or checking the more complex algorithms and reductions. The practical instantiation of the prediction model is especially underspecified.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate. The conclusion mentions open questions but does not seriously discuss the risks of using predicted advice in allocation systems, the consequences of misspecified utilities, strategic behavior, unequal prediction quality across agents, or fairness failures when advice is wrong.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent and useful map of online fair division under different future-information models, covering no information, normalization/total-value information, frequency predictions, noisy variants, and identical valuations. The resulting table of possibilities and impossibilities is a meaningful contribution.

The technical core appears sound. Algorithm 1 gives clean certificate-based PROP1 guarantees for all n and EF1 for two agents under normalization information, with matching or near-matching impossibility results for stronger notions. The frequency-prediction meta-algorithm is elegant: it reduces online allocation to an offline share guarantee via identically ordered instances and picking sequences.

The results are significant for the online fair-division literature. They clarify exactly what total-value information can buy, improve on prior MMS-only perspectives by addressing EF1/PROP1/EFX, and connect naturally to learning-augmented online algorithms.

The manuscript is well situated in related work, including prior normalized-valuation results, frequency-prediction models, online scheduling analogies, and recent fair-division literature. I also appreciate the correction of a flaw in an earlier claimed PROP1 impossibility.

Reproducibility is adequate for a theoretical paper: algorithms are given in pseudocode, running-time comments are included, and most claims are accompanied by full proofs. The assumptions about adaptive adversaries and ex post guarantees are stated clearly, and the appendix clarifies why the deterministic lower bounds extend to randomized algorithms in this model.
weaknesses: The learning-augmented frequency-prediction guarantee is somewhat weak as stated. The relative error depends on the induced online instantiation error, but the paper does not provide a substantive bound for natural instantiation rules beyond suggesting nearest matching. As a result, the theorem is more of a stability statement conditional on a good matching than a full learning-augmented guarantee.

The frequency-prediction model is powerful and somewhat stylized: knowing each agent's exact multiset of future item values can be close to knowing much of the instance, even though order and cross-agent correlations are hidden. The paper motivates this via type counts, but the practical plausibility and limits of this advice model deserve more careful discussion.

Some constructive claims depend on access to offline algorithms for the relevant feasible shares. This is reasonable, but the computational status is not uniformly spelled out for all instantiated shares; the statement "whenever the offline share is achievable in polynomial time" leaves part of the algorithmic reproducibility delegated to external results.

The presentation is generally clear but dense. Several long lower-bound proofs are hard to parse, and the paper would benefit from more intuition before the most intricate adversarial constructions, especially in the EFX impossibility and identical-valuations sections.

The paper has no explicit ethics or limitations section. The conclusion mentions open problems and model extensions, but a clearer discussion of limitations, including the strength of advice assumptions and the implications of deploying fair allocation policies with predicted valuations, would improve the manuscript.
